assumptions.summary: The nine indices describe three related families: centralizing, connecting, and spreading.
A particle moves one edge per second, splits at branches, and later reach is attenuated.
The same testing timespan T is used for all vertices; unreachable half-network reach is infinity.
Within-group indices are assumed correlated and normalized before PCA.
The impact measurement uses alpha=beta=gamma=1/3 for the displayed ranking.
The sixteen-paper citation data are selected to contain sufficient relations.
The user network edge weight combines shared movies with comment-score similarity.

language_observations.summary: The human style comes from semantic definitions, visible failure and repair, concrete graph/figure readings, a paradox resolved by local topology, immediate data prerequisites, and a conclusion narrowed by weaknesses.

the Summary compresses nine measures into three semantic families: Name the three network characteristics, list their sub-characteristics, state PCA and the weighted impact measure, then close with datasets and a bounded recommendation.

information overload turns a vague impact problem into a modeling program: Start with researchers filtering a mass of papers, reject single-factor analysis as insufficient, and announce new indices, validation, visualization, and utility as one program.

background separates structural description, quantitative parameters, algorithms, and dimension reduction: Move from who studies network structure to who quantifies it, who modifies algorithms, and who makes a comprehensive appraisal possible.

each characteristic family is defined by the network question it answers: Describe centralizing as structural position, connecting as integrity, and spreading as information dissemination before assigning indices.

a one-sided degree view triggers eigenvector centrality: State that degree alone can miss a high-degree node linked to weak neighbors, then add eigenvector centrality as another angle before PageRank iteration.
a particle-spreading analogy becomes two new indices: Release a particle, count occupied vertices and distance over time, attenuate later reach, and define breadth, half-network period, and depth.

an explicitly inaccurate approximation is retained only to derive a factor: Use an average-degree recurrence, say that the resulting score cannot be accepted, and keep the approximation only for choosing the attenuation factor before returning to the original definition.

bounds and an infinity case make the spreading indices interpretable: Give lower and upper bounds, constrain the testing timespan, and define the half-network period as infinity when a component cannot reach half the graph.
correlated indices are compressed before a weighted final score: Normalize three groups, apply PCA within each group, and add centralizing, connecting, and spreading vectors with explicit weights.

preprocessing decisions are followed by global statistics and visual readings: Remove indirect or isolated authors, report graph statistics, and read component and degree plots into a decision to analyze the network.

a degree-versus-impact paradox is resolved through the three score components and a local graph: Ask why a large citation node ranks low, inspect normalized characteristic curves and a detailed citation neighborhood, and explain the bottleneck role of the top-ranked node.

applications are mapped to new nodes and edges but immediately expose missing data: Transfer the graph to researchers and departments, specify cooperative edges and candidate weights, and list the counts, scales, times, and co-citations required to make the mapping credible.
a distributional reading supports a bounded utility claim: Read a user score distribution as roughly Gaussian, connect influential users to website attention, and retain the sample and proxy limits.

the conclusion pairs a broad contribution with explicit static, data, and weight weaknesses: State comprehensive evaluation, self-defined standards, classification, and visualization, then disclose time, sample, and weight limits before restating the model's contribution.

source.title: A Three-dimensional Network Impact Analysis Model Based on Centralizing, Connecting and Spreading Characteristics

source_quality.summary: All 20 pages were read and visually reviewed. The paper moves from information overload and semantic network classification through particle indices, PCA, graph applications, a topology-based citation explanation, and explicit static/data/weight limits.

decisions: which semantic family answers the network question
when an approximation must be rejected
whether a rank paradox is explained by local topology
what data and limits constrain transfer
inputs: coauthor graph, centrality indices, node-removal distances, particle spreading, PCA groups, citation links, department/user mappings
outputs: three family scores, IM ranks, paper ranks, transfer mappings, user distribution, and utility claims

title: A Three-dimensional Network Impact Analysis Model Based on Centralizing, Connecting and Spreading Characteristics
unresolved_questions: The paper reconstructs a multi-factor research-network objective but the official prompt wording is unavailable and the target impact concept remains broad.
Degree notation D is reused for total vertices, edge-count relation, and average degree; PageRank damping, normalization, and component policy are not fully specified.
Betweenness assumes shortest-path flow and clustering averages only degree-at-least-two vertices; tie weights and disconnected behavior are not reported.
Node-removal loss relies on pre/post distance matrices and an infinity convention, but the graph, distance implementation, and removal sensitivity are not released.
The average-degree particle recurrence is explicitly inaccurate for the final score; the corrected attenuation is still a stylized diffusion assumption.
Breadth bounds and an infinite half-network period for unreachable components are useful conventions, not uncertainty or calibrated time-scale evidence.
Depth uses d(t)-d(t-1)=1 and diameter normalization; the approximation and choice of T are not empirically justified.
PCA assumes within-group correlation and the displayed IM uses equal weights; covariance, retained variance, training data, and weight sensitivity are absent.
The Erdos1 graph removes indirect and isolated authors before analysis, so the 474-node, five-component sample is a selected population rather than a census.
Repeated top-author overlap and the ALON result are descriptive checks on the same score family, not independent validation of influence.
The sixteen-paper citation sample is selected for sufficient relations and the edge provenance, duplicate rule, and collection date are not reproducibly frozen.
The department and researcher transfers are hypothetical mappings that list needed cooperation, project, time, and co-citation data but do not supply them.
The 971-user graph and roughly Gaussian impact plot rely on scraped movie comments and a visual resemblance; no goodness-of-fit or external activity outcome is shown.
The conclusion admits static-network limits, a roughly one-thousand-person test, and imprecise equal weights; these constrain any general application claim.
